query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor concentration (on the order of ~5 at.%) of tin (Sn) to equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr will enhance its resistance to oxygen attack without degrading the alloy’s useful room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C
generation.intervention: Modify the composition by adding approximately 5 at.% Sn during alloy processing.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours with subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and elevated temperatures; keeping strain rate in the range 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹ during high-temperature measurements.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a Sn-enriched sublayer at the metal-oxide interface during high-temperature exposure.
generation.mechanism: During high-temperature exposure in air, Sn tends to segregate to the substrate–oxide scale interface. This Sn-enriched interlayer promotes the formation of a more adherent, slow-growing oxide scale, which reduces oxygen diffusion into the bulk material and mitigates pesting behavior, all while keeping the underlying microstructure responsible for good ductility and strength unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Sn-modified alloy will exhibit a significantly improved oxidation resistance (evidenced by lower oxygen uptake and better oxide scale adhesion) relative to the untreated alloy, while maintaining similar levels of tensile ductility and yield strength at both room temperature and at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: The untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy, which suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance under high-temperature (800 °C) air exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for exposures up to 5 hours at 800 °C in air and under similar mechanical loadings; the effects under longer exposures or at significantly higher temperature ranges remain to be tested.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Sn concentration and its potential long-term effects on microstructural stability and mechanical performance require further study. It is also uncertain whether Sn addition might interact with other oxide-forming elements during prolonged exposures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one group of standard equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and a second group with ~5 at.% Sn added. Subject both groups to air exposure at 800 °C for 5 hours under identical conditions. Then, perform post-exposure evaluations including oxide scale characterization and mechanical testing (tensile ductility and yield strength).
measurements: Oxide scale thickness, continuity, and adhesion (via microscopy and weight gain measurements)
Quantification of oxygen uptake (by thermogravimetric analysis and depth profiling)
Tensile tests to measure room-temperature ductility and yield strength, as well as high-temperature mechanical performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Sn-added samples do not show statistically significant improvements in oxidation resistance (i.e., similar or higher oxygen uptake, less adherent oxide scales) or if they display a significant degradation in tensile ductility or yield strength compared to the control samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,].
